verdictBasis: 0 blockers, 0 SHOULD-FIX, which is the ACCEPT bar. Codex's v41 blocker was correct and is repaired: the Ed25519 public key is now carried in a pinned encoding, joined by digest to the allowlist root and to both records, and consumed by verification. correctionToMyPriorVerdict.what: I returned ACCEPT on v41. Codex returned REJECT with PTCB-V41-B1. Codex was right and my ACCEPT was wrong.
correctionToMyPriorVerdict.whatIMissed: v41 specified Ed25519 verification under 'the 32-byte key whose digest is builderRootDigest', and the builderRoot allowlist member is DIGEST-BOUND, so the carrier held a SHA-256 digest of the public key and never the key itself. SHA-256 is preimage-resistant, so no verifier could obtain the key from what was carried, and the verification step as written could not be executed. I traced the digest binding chain — builderRootDigest equal to the member's identityEvidence.digest, to the signed object's field, to the later event's field — confirmed it was internally consistent, and never asked where the key bytes themselves come from. My v41 verdict even lists an adversarial checklist covering forgery, replay, root substitution and format confusion, and none of those items asks whether the verifier possesses the operands.
correctionToMyPriorVerdict.thePattern: This is my second ACCEPT that Codex correctly rejected, after v36, and the two share one shape. At v36 I checked what malformed input would refuse and not what a well-formed planted input would do. Here I checked that the bindings agreed with each other and not whether the operation had its inputs. Both are the same underlying error: verifying that a construction is internally coherent rather than that it can actually be executed against an adversary. I have applied the corresponding check explicitly this round and recorded its results below.
correctionToMyPriorVerdict.whatItChanges: The frozen Claude v41 ACCEPT stands unedited; this record is the correction. A coordinator weighing the v41 divergence should treat the Codex REJECT as the correct verdict for that generation and should discount my v41 ACCEPT as independent confirmation. It does not change any earlier verdict, and this generation is assessed on its own bytes.

repairsVerified.finding: PTCB-V41-B1 — the verifier had a key digest but no acquisition or same-object join for the public-key bytes
repairsVerified.result: REPAIRED, and by the first of the two routes Codex offered, which is the simpler and less failure-prone one. builderPublicKey now reads 'exact 32 raw Ed25519 public-key bytes. On the signed/later records encoded as 64-hex lowercase of those 32 bytes. SHA-256 of the 32 bytes MUST equal builderRoot.identityEvidence.digest AND signedObject.builderRootDigest AND later.builderRootDigest. Ed25519 verify MUST use these identical 32 bytes as the public key. Absent, not 32 bytes, or digest mismatch refuses.' That supplies the encoding Codex asked to pin, the three-way digest join, the requirement that verification consume those identical bytes, and the absent-key and non-32-byte refusals. verify is rewritten to name the operand — 'Ed25519 verify of the 64-byte builderSignature under builderPublicKey (the same 32 bytes hashed above)' — so the operation and its input are stated together. Codex's same-event association sub-requirement is moot under this route rather than unmet: the key is carried inline on the signed record and mirrored on the later event with 'MUST equal signedObject.builderPublicKey', so there is no run-time acquisition event to associate. The closed forms were updated to match, which is where I have most often found propagation failures: linuxForm is restated as 'exactly {tag, pathlessObservation, measuredBootTranscriptDigest, kexecCapability, builderRoot, builderPublicKey, builderSignature, builderRootDigest} plus ikconfigDigest on the IKCONFIG present branch. extrasRejected', and laterEventVariant carries builderPublicKey, builderSignature and builderRootDigest with fieldwise equalities. The vector classes Codex named are reserved, including absent key, non-32-byte key, digest mismatch and correct-key-verifies.

repairsVerified.finding: PTCB-V41-S1 — the governing IKCONFIG branch did not define unmatched, reversed or extra-marker disposition
repairsVerified.result: REPAIRED, over every malformed class Codex enumerated. markers now reads 'Count every IKCFG_ST and IKCFG_ED occurrence in P. Absent condition: zero ST and zero ED. Present condition: exactly one ST and exactly one ED, ST byte-offset strictly less than ED, interval wholly inside P. Lone ST, lone ED, reversed (ED before ST), nested, overlapping, or any extra marker beyond one ST and one ED refuses.' The two branches are then keyed to those exact conditions rather than to the looser any-pair and zero-pairs wording, and the reserved vectors include lone ST, reversed markers and one pair plus a stray ED.

residualTrustNamedExplicitly.whatRemains: A builder holding the key whose SHA-256 is builderRootDigest can sign an attestation asserting kexec-absent for an image that is not. No clause detects that and none claims to.
residualTrustNamedExplicitly.andOneLevelUp: The signer of the TCB inventory chooses which builder root is allowlisted and now also carries the builder's public key on the signed object. A malicious closure signer could therefore name a builder key it controls. That is not a defect introduced here — it is the base trust of the signed closure, on which every other clause in this contract already depends — but it means the builder and closure roles are separated by policy rather than by mechanism, and a coordinator should read the separation that way.
residualTrustNamedExplicitly.whatIsOutOfScope: Key management for the builder root, including issuance, rotation and revocation, and whether one operator controls both the builder key and the closure-signing key.

summary: ACCEPT at 0 blockers and 0 SHOULD-FIX, with a correction recorded first. My v41 ACCEPT was wrong and Codex's v41 REJECT was right: the contract specified Ed25519 verification under a key that the carrier never supplied, holding only its SHA-256, so the operation had no executable input. I had traced the digest bindings for consistency and never asked where the key bytes come from — the same shape as my v36 miss, where I asked what malformed input refuses and not what a well-formed planted input does. This round I ran that check explicitly across every step of the chain and record the trace. v42 closes the gap by the simpler of Codex's two routes: builderPublicKey carries the exact 32 raw bytes as 64-hex on both the signed object and the later event, SHA-256 of those bytes must equal the allowlist member's identityEvidence.digest and both record fields, verification must consume those identical bytes, and absent, wrong-size or digest-mismatched keys refuse. The closed linuxForm and laterEventVariant were both updated, which is the propagation step this row has historically missed. Codex's two SHOULD-FIX items are repaired in full: marker cardinality now counts every occurrence and refuses lone, reversed, nested, overlapping and stray cases with absence defined as zero of each, and architectureDispatch returns actualHeaderKind with preimage.headerKind required to equal it across all three mappings. Structure is clean throughout — 65 of 65 pins reproduce, 27 changed paths with zero off-roster, a pure-append reviewGuidance, a byte-exact register row, reproducing remeasurement pins, 39 of 39 D-096 occurrences refusals, one structural-proof standing and no stale live references. I found no second operand gap; the AK public key was already carried as TPMT_PUBLIC and the transcript rows live in the signed inventory rather than existing only as a digest. What remains is trust, named rather than hidden: the rooted builder can attest falsely, and one level up the closure signer both allowlists the builder root and carries its public key, so builder and closure roles are separated by policy rather than by mechanism. ACCEPT is a verdict on this candidate only, and given that two of my prior ACCEPTs on this row were wrong it should be weighed alongside the other reviewer's rather than relied on alone.
